title: Praise, not death
hook: the mourner's prayer praises God and never mentions death

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was the ghats at Varanasi, where death is kept in plain sight. Your line was kept in plain sight. Today, Jewish voices, and a mourner's prayer.

A mourner stands up in a synagogue, weeks after a funeral, and begins to speak in Aramaic. Around the room, people answer: amen. The prayer is the Kaddish, said by Jewish mourners for the people they have lost. Read it through, start to finish, and something is missing. It never mentions death. Not the person who died, not grief, not what comes after. Why is the mourner's prayer all praise?
screen: `A MOURNER STANDS.` → `THE ROOM ANSWERS: AMEN.` → `NO WORD ABOUT DEATH.`

segments.voice: First, the words. The Kaddish opens, yitgadal v'yitkadash sh'mei rabba: may God's great name be made great and holy. Then it keeps going: blessed, praised, glorified, lifted up. It even says God is beyond all the blessings and songs anyone can say. Second, the answer. The mourner doesn't carry it alone. The Kaddish is said with a minyan, a gathered quorum, and at its heart the whole room answers together: may his great name be blessed, forever and ever. Third, the ending. The last line asks for peace, for the people praying and for all Israel. It echoes a verse in the book of Job: "he maketh peace in his high places." Praise, then peace. And still no death. Fourth, why. Jewish teachers give more than one answer, and they don't cancel each other out. Some say the mourner, whose world has just gotten smaller, stands up in public and declares that God is still great: faith said aloud at the hardest moment. Tradition also holds that a child's Kaddish honors a parent who has died, so the praise is said on their behalf. And some point to the room: the community's answer pulls the mourner back into the circle, again and again. A person in grief may have no words of their own. The Kaddish hands them old words, about something larger than the loss, and a room full of people to say amen.
screen: `MAY HIS GREAT NAME BE GREAT.` · `THE ROOM ANSWERS TOGETHER.` · `IT ENDS IN PEACE.` · `WHY PRAISE, AND NOT DEATH?` · then, large: `PRAISE, NOT DEATH.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind a life: someone who has died, if there's someone you'd like to remember, or someone living, if that feels better today. Find one sentence of praise for that life, what was good in them, what they gave, what they made easier, and say it silently or quietly aloud. Then let the quiet hold it, the way a room holds the Kaddish.
Kaddish: the Jewish prayer said by mourners, mostly in Aramaic, that praises God, asks for peace, and never mentions death. Today's word.
Your line: faith said aloud. Praise, then peace, and a room to say amen. Day seven hundred seventy-three, done.

howItsDone: Jewish mourners say the Mourner's Kaddish at services with a minyan, during the period of mourning and on the anniversary of a death, and the congregation answers with amen and the response 'may his great name be blessed'.

notes: The Kaddish is paraphrased throughout; no translation quoted. The opening transliteration 'yitgadal v'yitkadash sh'mei rabba' follows common Ashkenazi/modern usage; confirm.
Job 25:2 quoted from the KJV; JPS 1917 could be used instead for the Jewish voices block if a reviewer prefers.
'Tradition also holds that a child's Kaddish honors a parent who has died, so the praise is said for them, on their behalf': confirm framing.
howItsDone mentions the mourning period and the anniversary (yahrzeit) without stating durations, by design. Customs differ across communities, including on who says Kaddish.
